title: Dollar thresholds in force since October 1, 2025, and the text that sets each
caption: Final rule 90 FR 41872 raised six thresholds on October 1, 2025 and left the bond, wage-rate and trade-agreements figures alone [340](#cite:340) [417](#cite:417). Each row gives the figure now in the text named, the figure it replaced where the rule states one, and the text that prints it. Where two official texts disagree the table gives both. 13 CFR 125.3 still prints $750,000 and $1,500,000 for subcontracting plans against $900,000 and $2 million in FAR 19.702 [704](#cite:704) [692](#cite:692). 13 CFR 124.506 prints $7,000,000, $4,500,000 and $25,000,000 for 8(a) awards against $8.5 million, $5.5 million and $30 million in the FAR [331](#cite:331) [338](#cite:338) [339](#cite:339). 10 U.S.C. 3702 reads $10,000,000 for defense prime contracts entered into after June 30, 2026, against $2.5 million in FAR 15.403-4 [1036](#cite:1036) [1325](#cite:1325). Construction bonds start above $150,000 in the FAR and above $100,000 in the statute as read [644](#cite:644) [947](#cite:947). Other dollar gates, such as the $25,000 notice line [562](#cite:562) and the trafficking compliance plan [654](#cite:654), are in the gate records and are not repeated here.
how_to_read: Read across a row: the threshold, the figure in force, the figure before October 1, 2025, and the text that prints it. Where you see the same threshold on two rows, two official texts disagree; the status column tells you whether one text lags, or whether the second figure applies only to defense contracts. A blank in the prior column means the references read do not state an earlier figure. It does not mean there was none. The governing text named in each row is where the figure is printed.

explain.text: The figure was changed by the inflation-adjustment rule, FAR Case 2024-001, published August 27, 2025 and effective October 1, 2025 [417](#cite:417) [340](#cite:340).

Two official texts print different figures for the same threshold. The table shows both and does not pick one. For subcontracting plans and the 8(a) figures the second text is an SBA regulation in Title 13 [704](#cite:704) [331](#cite:331).

The rule names these thresholds as left out of the adjustment: Construction Wage Rate Requirements, Service Contract Labor Standards, performance and payment bonds, and trade agreements [340](#cite:340).

label: Figure 2
title: SBIR/STTR Phase I and Phase II amounts as posted, by agency and source

y.label: Posted amount (US dollars; upper bound where a range is posted)

caption: Phase I and Phase II amounts as each source posted them when read on October 3, 2026, one row per source. The SBA Policy Directive sets base guidelines of $150,000 and $1,000,000 [5](#cite:5), and SBIR.gov says that as of April 2026 agencies may go to $323,090 and $2,153,927 without seeking SBA approval [11](#cite:11). Agency pages differ from SBA's agency cards and from each other. The Army's How It Works page gives Phase I up to $300,000 and its Phases page gives up to $250K [81](#cite:81) [82](#cite:82). AFWERX's Get Funded page gives up to $323,000 and $2.1 million; its Open Topic page gives $75K and $1.25M for SBIR [64](#cite:64) [67](#cite:67). DHS limits Phase I to $100,000 on its own page where SBA's card says $175,000 [196](#cite:196) [12](#cite:12). NASA's solicitation gives $225,000 and its Phase II page $1,275,000 where SBA's card says $150,000 and $1 Million [169](#cite:169) [172](#cite:172) [12](#cite:12). Rows labelled SBA tutorial are older SBIR.gov tutorial pages; they are kept because the Navy's amounts appear nowhere else in the references read [57](#cite:57). The Missile Defense Agency's page posts durations but no amounts and is not plotted [90](#cite:90).
how_to_read: Each row is one source for one agency or component; the two bars are its Phase I and Phase II figures. Compare rows that share an agency name to see where sources disagree. A bar shows a ceiling or a typical figure as the source words it, not what any one award paid; the qualifier column tells you which. Where a source posts a range, the bar is drawn at the upper end. A missing bar means that source did not give a figure for that phase.

explain.on: series: Phase I and Phase II
explain.text: Phase I tests feasibility and Phase II continues the work. The directive gives base guidelines of $150,000 and $1,000,000, including modifications, and lets agencies go higher within limits [5](#cite:5).
The card SBIR.gov shows for each participating agency. Its figures are often older or rounder than the agency's own page or solicitation [12](#cite:12).
Individual-agency tutorial pages on SBIR.gov. They are undated and the records treat them as historical [57](#cite:57) [58](#cite:58) [126](#cite:126).
NIH components may set budgets above the guideline. The parent announcement tables run from the SBA guideline up to $700,000 for Phase I and $3,000,000 for Phase II [137](#cite:137).

The published figure in whole dollars. For a range it is the upper bound; where a page gives separate SBIR and STTR figures it is the SBIR figure; where a base and an option are given it is the base. The amount_as_published column keeps the original wording.

source: Amounts are as published on the page, card or solicitation named in each row, read October 3, 2026, with units and wording kept in amount_as_published. The amount_usd column restates one figure per row in whole dollars for plotting (upper bound of a range; SBIR figure where SBIR and STTR differ; base where an option is listed). No other conversion; no averaging across sources.

label: Figure 3
title: DoD other transaction obligations by fiscal year, as GAO reports them

y.label: Obligations (US dollars, billions, as GAO reports them)

caption: GAO puts DoD's obligations through prototype and production other transactions at over $18 billion in fiscal year 2024, with prototype agreements over $16 billion and production through follow-on authority $2 billion [1121] [1070]. For fiscal years 2021 to 2024 together it reports $62.9 billion, of which prototype agreements were $56.3 billion, or 90 percent [1121]. The consortia-based part is the only one reported year by year in the references read: $5,218.5 million, $12,644.6 million and $6,474.8 million for fiscal years 2019 to 2021 in the 2022 report [1119](#cite:1119), and $8.1 billion, $6.0 billion, $7.1 billion and $7.0 billion for fiscal years 2021 to 2024 in the 2025 report [1121](#cite:1121). The two reports give different figures for fiscal year 2021 and neither reference says why. As shares, GAO gives consortia nearly two-thirds of prototype dollars in fiscal years 2019 to 2021 and about half of prototype obligations in 2021 to 2024; both are period figures, not yearly ones [1071](#cite:1071) [1121](#cite:1121). Not plotted: GAO's totals for fiscal years 2016 and 2021, and the yearly totals the sweep read off the report's Figure 2, because the recheck could not confirm them on the page read [1070](#cite:1070).
how_to_read: Each bar is one figure from one GAO report for one fiscal year; the legend tells you which report and which measure. Only fiscal year 2024 has a total, and it is published as "over $18 billion", so that bar marks a floor and not an exact value. The other years show only the part that ran through consortia. Where you see two consortia bars for fiscal year 2021, the two reports disagree. You cannot read a trend in total obligations from this chart, because the earlier totals are not in it.

explain.text: Obligations on other transactions awarded through a consortium, where DoD awards a base agreement to a management organization and the manager issues a sub-award to the member chosen [1119](#cite:1119).

GAO states these as lower bounds ("over $18 billion", "over $16 billion"). The bar is drawn at the stated floor; the true figure is higher by an amount the references do not give [1121](#cite:1121) [1070](#cite:1070).
The 2022 report gives $6,474.8 million and the 2025 report $8.1 billion for consortia-based obligations in the same year. Both are shown as published [1119](#cite:1119) [1121](#cite:1121).

The share is stated for a span of years, not per year: nearly two-thirds of prototype dollars for fiscal years 2019 to 2021, and about half of prototype obligations for 2021 to 2024 [1071](#cite:1071) [1121](#cite:1121).

Whether the reference says a value was read off a chart in the report. None of the plotted rows is marked that way; the values that were read off GAO's Figure 2 failed the recheck and are left out [1070](#cite:1070).

source: Values are as published in GAO-22-105357 (Table 1) and GAO-25-107546, kept in the as_published column. Figures given in millions of dollars were divided by 1,000 to put every bar on one axis in billions; no inflation adjustment and no other conversion was made. Figures published as "over" are plotted at the stated floor and flagged in the qualifier column.

label: Figure 4
title: Posted membership dues and fees on awards, by consortium
caption: Posted dues and fees on awards for the 21 consortia whose pages gave a figure when read on October 3 and 4, 2026, with the manager and sponsor each names. Dues run from nothing (JDEC, NSTIC, RRPV, Cornerstone, and DIBC in its first year) to $10,000 a year at the top of NSTXL's revenue scale [1138](#cite:1138) [1193](#cite:1193) [1215](#cite:1215) [1235](#cite:1235) [1191](#cite:1191). Where a rate on awards is posted it runs from 0.05% of awarded funding at NSTIC to 0.15% at AMTC and 0.5% at DOTC and NEST [1194](#cite:1194) [1169](#cite:1169). The CMG consortia state a fixed-percentage fee without a rate; the only rate found, 4.3%, is from C5's 2017 base agreement [1220](#cite:1220) [1222](#cite:1222) [1224](#cite:1224). NSTXL says it takes nothing from the performer and is paid a management fee by the Government [1142](#cite:1142). On the 12 agreements GAO reviewed, managers' compensation ran from 0.7% to 21.3% of obligated dollars [1119](#cite:1119). A blank cell means no figure was posted on the pages read. Consortia with no posted figure at all are left out (MSTIC, EMC2, MATAC, DAF TENCAP, NSC, BioMaP, HSTech, SOSSEC, SCEC, UCAH, DATC and DEC); their records say what was and was not found.
how_to_read: Each row is one consortium. Read the dues column for what you would pay to belong and the fee column for what is taken when a project is awarded; the two are separate charges and a consortium may post one, both or neither. A blank is not a zero: it means the pages read gave no figure. Where the manager or sponsor cell is blank, the note says what the sources disagreed on.

explain.text: The organization that runs the consortium under a base agreement with the government. GAO names four main ones: ATI, CMG, NSTXL and SOSSEC [1119](#cite:1119).
What the consortium's own join or membership page states, in its words. NSTXL charges one membership for every agreement it manages, scaled by annual revenue [1138](#cite:1138) [1142](#cite:1142).

explain.on: column: Fee on awards as posted
explain.text: A charge assessed on project awards, stated as a percentage of awarded funding where a rate is given. Several consortia state that an assessment applies without giving the rate [1178](#cite:1178) [1183](#cite:1183) [1204](#cite:1204).
The 0.15% assessment appears on two pages with different effective dates: October 1, 2020 on the AMTC FAQ and October 1, 2023 on the NAC FAQ [1172](#cite:1172) [1169](#cite:1169).
The dues figure comes from 2022 industry-day slides hosted by a third party and is not on the current site [1227](#cite:1227).

label: Figure 5
title: Statutory small-business goals and reported results, fiscal years 2024 and 2025
caption: The statute sets governmentwide goals of not less than 23 percent of prime contract awards for small business, 5 percent each for small disadvantaged, women-owned and service-disabled veteran-owned firms, and 3 percent for HUBZone firms [374](#cite:374). SBA's January 2025 release, described there as preliminary, put fiscal year 2024 at 28.78, 12.26, 4.97, 5.15 and 2.74 percent [381](#cite:381). For fiscal year 2025 the Congressional Research Service's table gives 27.58, 11.60, 4.52, 5.01 and 2.66 percent [378](#cite:378). SBA's June 2026 release gives nearly 28 percent for small business (27.9 as extracted) and 11.6 percent for small disadvantaged firms, says service-disabled veteran-owned firms were over the 5 percent target, and gives no women-owned or HUBZone figure [382](#cite:382). The sources differ in small ways and both are shown: the 2026 release restates the fiscal year 2024 small disadvantaged figure as 12.27 percent against 12.26, and its small business share for 2025 is above the CRS figure [382](#cite:382) [381](#cite:381) [378](#cite:378). The two SBA releases were not re-read in the recheck pass.
how_to_read: Each group of bars is one category of firm. The grey bar is the floor the statute sets; the coloured bars are what was reported for fiscal years 2024 and 2025. A coloured bar taller than the grey one means the reported share was above the goal. Where you see two bars for the same year, two sources gave different figures. There is no SBA bar for women-owned or HUBZone firms in 2025 because the release did not give one.

explain.text: The governmentwide floors in 15 U.S.C. 644(g): small business not less than 23 percent of prime contract awards; the statute states the service-disabled veteran goal as a share of prime and subcontract awards [374](#cite:374).
From SBA's release of January 10, 2025, which called the numbers preliminary prime contracting figures. The final scorecard for that year was not among the references read [381](#cite:381).

From a Congressional Research Service Insight dated June 30, 2026; the five percentages were confirmed against its Table 2 on recheck. It is the only reference with women-owned and HUBZone figures for the year [378](#cite:378).
The release words the small business share as "nearly 28%"; the 27.9 plotted is the figure as extracted from the same release, which was not re-read on recheck [382](#cite:382).
SBA's February 2025 release says the SDB goal was returned to its statutory level of 5 percent; the statute's floor is the grey bar [317](#cite:317) [374](#cite:374).

label: Figure 6
title: From where a firm stands to the routes that fit
caption: A decision flow built from the situation tags on the route and program records. A firm starts from one of five situations; each leads to the route families that hold at least one route tagged for it, and each family opens onto its main routes with the text that governs them. A firm that is not yet registered meets the SAM.gov gate first, because registration is required when submitting an offer and at award [303](#cite:303). Set-asides and the certified programs rest on FAR Part 19 and 15 U.S.C. 644 [384](#cite:384) [374](#cite:374) [338](#cite:338) [349](#cite:349) [368](#cite:368) [357](#cite:357). SBIR and STTR rest on 15 U.S.C. 638, the SBA Policy Directive and Pub. L. 119-83 [3](#cite:3) [5](#cite:5) [1](#cite:1). Other transactions and commercial solutions openings rest on 10 U.S.C. 4021, 4022 and 3458 [1031](#cite:1031) [1028](#cite:1028) [1033](#cite:1033). Partnering routes rest on FAR subpart 9.6, 13 CFR Parts 121 and 125, and 10 U.S.C. 4902 [761](#cite:761) [770](#cite:770) [773](#cite:773) [785](#cite:785) [451](#cite:451). This is a conceptual figure: it shows which routes the records tag for each situation, not which routes any one firm qualifies for.
how_to_read: Start at the left with the situation closest to yours and follow its lines to the route families; a thicker line means more of the routes shown carry that situation tag. Each family box fans out to its main routes on the right. A route box names the record to open, and the record names the governing text. If you are not yet registered, the gate box above that situation comes before any route.

explain.text: The five starting points the pathfinder asks about: not yet registered, registered with no award, first awards and growing, holding a technology that needs funding, and looking for partners. They are the situations tags on the records.
The four families of routes the guide is organised by: set-asides and vehicles, SBIR/STTR and innovation front doors, other transactions and commercial solutions openings, and primes and partnering.
Drawn where at least one of the routes shown is tagged for that situation in routes.yaml or programs.yaml. The routes list on each edge in the data file names them.
An offeror is required to be registered in SAM when submitting an offer or quotation and at time of award; registration generates the Unique Entity ID [303](#cite:303) [608](#cite:608).
One route or program record each, with its governing text. The 26 shown are the main routes of each family; the records hold the rest, including the agency programs and the individual consortia.

source: Conceptual figure drawn by the builder. Nodes and edges are in figures/data/route-decision.json; the situation and family of each route are taken from the situations and family fields of routes.yaml and programs.yaml as of October 3, 2026, and the governing texts from the governing_text field or the cited statute or regulation. No values were converted. Which 26 routes count as main is an editorial choice.

pathway.note: Conceptual. Situation-to-family edges exist where at least one of the route nodes shown carries that situation tag in routes.yaml or programs.yaml; the routes list on each edge names them. Family follows the family field of the record. Refs are the governing texts of each route.

label: Figure 7
title: What changed, December 2024 to October 2026, by status
caption: The 51 dated changes recorded between December 2024 and October 2026, placed by date and by status: final, class deviation, pending implementation, proposed or announced. The series says how each is sourced. Most of the anchors of this guide moved inside the window: the order for the FAR overhaul (April 15, 2025) [386](#cite:386), the threshold rise (October 1, 2025) [417](#cite:417), the fiscal year 2026 defense authorization act (December 18, 2025) [1273](#cite:1273) [1033](#cite:1033), the SBIR and STTR reauthorization (April 13, 2026) [1](#cite:1), the CMMC Phase II suspension (announced July 13, 2026) [625](#cite:625) and the 8(a) rule (final August 11, 2026, effective September 10, 2026) [314](#cite:314). Eight items are known here only from secondary sources or from texts that could not be read, and they are marked as such. Left off the chart: one record dated only to the year 2025, NSF Translation to Practice [1401](#cite:1401), and three records dated outside the window.
how_to_read: Time runs left to right and each row is a status, so you can see at a glance what is law (final), what is in use by deviation, what is enacted but not yet implemented, and what is only proposed or announced. Each point is one change record; points stacked at one date happened on the same day. Check the series before you rely on a point: anything not marked as read from a primary text is reported, not confirmed. A point shows when a change was made or announced, which is not always when it takes effect.

explain.text: The status word on the change record. Final means a law, final rule or completed action; class-deviation means agencies follow new text while the codified text stays in force; pending-implementation means enacted with no implementing document found; proposed and announced carry no legal effect yet.

How the record is sourced: primary (the governing text or official page was read), primary-partial (read in part), secondary-only (reported by commentary only), unread (the text is listed but could not be read) or unconfirmed (not confirmed as live).

Ten records share December 18, 2025: nine on the fiscal year 2026 defense authorization act and one on DoD class deviations dated the same day. Sections 1802, 1823 and 1804 were verified in the U.S. Code [1273](#cite:1273) [1033](#cite:1033) [1036](#cite:1036); sections 1822, 1824 and 824 were read as headings only and their content comes from digests [806](#cite:806) [1108](#cite:1108).
The date field of the record. Three records give only a month and are placed on its first day; the date_precision column marks them.

The FAR overhaul reaches contracts this way for now: model text is issued part by part and adopted agency by agency. Part 19 was taken up by GSA from November 3, 2025 and by DoD from February 1, 2026 [400](#cite:400) [402](#cite:402).

source: One row per record in changes.yaml dated from December 2024 to October 2026; date, status, basis and sources are copied from the record and the short title is the builder's. Month-only dates are plotted on the first of the month (plot_date) with the original kept in date. Nothing else was converted.

label: Figure 8
title: SBIR/STTR from Phase I to Phase III, with the branches around it
caption: SBIR and STTR run in three phases. Phase I tests feasibility, with a base guideline of $150,000; Phase II continues the work, with a base guideline of $1,000,000; Phase III is work that derives from, extends or completes the earlier work and is paid from other funds, with no limit on number, duration, type or dollar value [5](#cite:5). As of April 2026 agencies may go to $323,090 and $2,153,927 without seeking SBA approval [11](#cite:11). Around that line sit the branches. Direct to Phase II skips Phase I on a written determination of demonstrated feasibility and now runs until September 30, 2031 at NIH, DoD, Education, DOE and NASA [5](#cite:5) [1](#cite:1). Fast-Track, at NSF, joins a $400,000 Phase I component to a Phase II of up to $1,155,000 in one award [35](#cite:35). One sequential Phase II may follow the first [5](#cite:5). The Strategic Breakthrough award is not more than $30,000,000 over not more than 48 months and needs at least one prior Phase II award and not less than 100 percent matching funds [1](#cite:1). After Phase II, agency transition programs add money or help: TACFI and STRATFI [236](#cite:236), Army CATALYST [239](#cite:239), the Navy's STP [235](#cite:235), ART [55](#cite:55), APFIT [108](#cite:108) [109](#cite:109), NIH's Commercialization Readiness Pilot [31](#cite:31) and NSF's Phase IIB supplement [35](#cite:35). An agency may award Phase III sole source under 15 U.S.C. 638(r)(4) [225](#cite:225).
how_to_read: Follow the heavy line left to right for the standard path: Phase I, Phase II, Phase III. The boxes above and below Phase I are other ways in, and both arrive at Phase II. The boxes after Phase II are what can follow it before or alongside Phase III; the list under the transition box names the agency programs. Open a box in the app to see its amounts, time limits and the text behind them. The figure shows what the rules allow, not what any agency will fund in a given year.

explain.text: Not a third award from the SBIR budget. It is any work that derives from, extends or completes Phase I or II work, funded from other sources, and the size limits for Phases I and II do not apply to it [5](#cite:5).
The posted directive still lists only NIH, DoD and Education and an expired date; Pub. L. 119-83 extended the authority to September 30, 2031 and added DOE, NASA and STTR [5](#cite:5) [1](#cite:1).

A new tier in the 2026 act for agencies whose required SBIR spending exceeds $100,000,000. Defense awards carry extra conditions, including a commitment from a senior acquisition official [1](#cite:1).
NIH also offers Fast-Track and counts those applications in its per-firm limit of nine a fiscal year [31](#cite:31) [29](#cite:29).

Each has its own eligibility and matching rule. APFIT is procurement funding that only a government organisation can request on a firm's behalf; the firm must be a small business, a nontraditional defense contractor, or one with no more than $400,000,000 in contracts in the prior year [109](#cite:109).

source: Conceptual figure drawn by the builder. Nodes and edges are in figures/data/sbir-phases.json. Amounts and durations in the node details are as the cited statute, directive and agency pages give them; nothing was converted. The transition programs shown are those with a program record in this pack and are not a complete list.

nodes.label: Strategic Breakthrough award
